dan01.q: A ball rolls onto the road from between two parked cars. What do you expect?
a: A child may run after it
The ball will roll away by itself, nothing else
Somebody may step out between the cars without looking
dan01.why: Where a ball comes, a child is often close behind – and it looks only at the ball. Brake at once and be ready to stop.

dan02.q: Children stand at the kerb ahead, playing. How do you behave?
a: Slow down and be ready to brake
Sound the horn and keep your speed
Keep more distance to the side if you can
dan02.why: With children about, drive so that they cannot come to harm – slowly, ready to stop, with room to the side. They may do something unexpected.

dan03.q: It is just above freezing. Where must you expect black ice first?
a: On bridges
In shady stretches through a forest
In a sunny town centre
dan03.why: Bridges cool from below as well, and forest shade keeps the sun off: there the road freezes first. Adapt your speed to the road.

dan04.q: Heavy rain, the water stands on the road and the steering suddenly feels light. What do you do?
a: Take your foot off the accelerator and hold the wheel straight
Brake hard at once
Steer sharply to the edge of the road
dan04.why: That is aquaplaning: the tyres float on the water. Do not brake or steer hard – let the car slow down until the tyres grip again. Drive slower where water stands.

dan05.q: The low sun dazzles you and you can hardly see the road ahead. What do you do?
a: Slow down so that you can stop within the distance you can see
Keep your speed: you know the road
Lower the sun visor
dan05.why: You may only drive as fast as lets you stop within the distance you can see. Dazzled, that distance is short.

dan06.q: A cyclist ahead of you looks back over his left shoulder. What may he be about to do?
a: Turn left or pull out to the left
Nothing: cyclists look round all the time
Swerve round an obstacle ahead of him
dan06.why: A look over the shoulder often comes before a move to the left. Keep back, do not overtake now, be ready to brake.

dan07.q: Somebody with a white stick stands at the edge of the road. What do you do?
a: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound the horn so that he hears you
Let him cross if he wants to
dan07.why: A white stick means the person cannot see well. Protect people who need help: slowly, ready to brake, and let them cross.

dan08.q: At night a person in dark clothes walks at the edge of a country road. When do you see him with dipped headlights?
a: Later than in the daytime – often only at about 25 m
As early as somebody in bright clothes
Only when the full beam is on
dan08.why: Dark clothes reflect little light: they are seen much later than light ones. Drive at night so that you can stop within the reach of your lights.

dan09.q: A sign warns of deer crossing; it is dusk. What is right?
a: Drive slower and watch the edges of the road
When a deer stands on the road: brake, dip the lights, sound the horn
Swerve round an animal whatever the cost
dan09.why: At dusk animals cross most often. Slow down; with an animal on the road brake hard, keep straight – swerving into a tree or the oncoming traffic is far worse.

dan10.q: A car ahead of you stops at the kerb in a narrow street. What must you expect?
a: A door may open on the driver's side
Somebody may get out and walk round the car
Nothing, it has stopped
dan10.why: Passing a car that just stopped, leave room for an opening door and watch for people stepping out.

dan11.q: You want to get out of your car parked at the kerb. What do you do first?
a: Look in the mirror and over your shoulder for cyclists and cars
Open the door quickly so that you are out of the way
Open the door with the far hand, so that you turn and look back
dan11.why: Getting in or out you must not endanger anybody. Opening the door with the hand away from it turns your body and your eyes back.

dan12.q: Leaves lie wet on the road in autumn. What changes?
a: The braking distance can become much longer
The tyres grip as well as on dry road
Cornering speed must come down
dan12.why: Wet leaves are as slippery as ice. Brake earlier and take bends more slowly.

dan13.q: Ahead, a lorry indicates right at a junction; a cycle lane runs beside it. What may happen?
a: It must wait for cyclists going straight on – and may stop suddenly
It may swing out to the left before turning right
It turns at once, cyclists must wait
dan13.why: Long vehicles swing out before turning and must let those going straight on go first. Keep your distance and do not squeeze past.

dan14.q: An older person crosses the road slowly, away from any crossing. What do you do?
a: Slow down and let her cross
Wait until she is safely on the pavement
Drive round her closely behind
dan14.why: Old people may stop, turn or stumble. Make sure no danger can arise for them – even when they do something unexpected.

dan15.q: Fog lies over the road and you see only about 40 m. What is right?
a: Drive no faster than 50 km/h – slower if need be
The rear fog light may be switched on
Use the full beam
dan15.why: When fog, snow or rain leave you less than 50 m to see, 50 km/h is the most. The rear fog light only then; full beam only lights up the fog.

dan16.q: You see this in the picture: three cars at a crossroads without signs. You are the car from below. Who goes first?
a: The car coming from your right
You
The car coming from your left
dan16.why: Right before left: the car on your right has nobody on its right – it goes first.

beh01.q: Behind you comes an ambulance with blue lights and siren. What do you do?
a: Make way at once
Keep going until the next junction
Stop at the edge if that clears the way
beh01.why: Blue lights together with the siren mean: everybody must make way at once.

beh02.q: On a motorway with three lanes the traffic slows to walking pace. You are in the middle lane. Where do you steer?
a: To the right, as far as the lane allows
To the left
Stay in the middle of the lane
beh02.why: The emergency corridor lies between the leftmost lane and the one next to it: the left lane moves left, all others move right.

beh03.q: Your lane ends ahead because of roadworks, the traffic is dense. Where do you change lanes?
a: Right where the lane ends, taking turns with the others
As early as possible, at the first gap
Not at all – the others must let you in first
beh03.why: Zip merging: drive on to where the lane ends; there the cars go in turn, one from each lane.

beh04.q: When must you use the right-hand lane of a road with several lanes outside town?
a: Always, as far as you can – the left lanes are for overtaking
Only on the motorway
Only with a slow vehicle
beh04.why: Keep as far right as you can. Outside town you overtake on the left and then return to the right.

beh05.q: You want to turn right. A cyclist on the cycle lane beside you goes straight on. Who goes first?
a: The cyclist
You, because you indicated first
Whoever is faster
beh05.why: Turning, you let those go straight on first who ride beside you on the cycle lane – also when they come from behind. Look over your shoulder.

beh06.q: You want to reverse out of a narrow driveway, you cannot see the road. What is right?
a: Ask somebody to guide you if you must
Reverse slowly, ready to stop at once
Reverse quickly so that you are in the way only briefly
beh06.why: Reversing you must make sure nobody can come to harm – get somebody to guide you if needed.

beh07.q: May you hold your mobile phone in your hand to read a message while driving?
a: No
Yes, at a red light with the engine running
Yes, for a quick glance
beh07.why: While driving you must not hold a phone. Use it only by voice or with a quick glance when it sits in its holder – and only with the vehicle stopped and the engine fully off may you take it in your hand.

beh08.q: You come upon an accident and nobody is helping yet. What do you do?
a: Make the place safe: hazard lights, warning triangle
Give first aid and call 112
Drive past slowly: others will help
beh08.why: Everybody must help as far as they can – failing to help is an offence. First make the place safe, then help, and call 112.

beh09.q: You touched a parked car while parking. Nobody is about. What do you do?
a: Wait a reasonable time for the owner
If nobody comes, tell the police
Leave a note and drive away
beh09.why: Whoever was involved in an accident must not leave the place without making it possible to know who they are. A note behind the wiper is not enough.

beh10.q: When may you sound the horn?
a: When you or others are in danger
Outside town, to say that you will overtake
To greet somebody
beh10.why: The horn is a warning: when danger threatens, and outside town to announce overtaking.

beh11.q: You want to change lanes. What must you do?
a: Look in the mirrors and over your shoulder
Indicate in good time
Change only if nobody can be put in danger
beh11.why: Changing lanes is allowed only when nobody can be endangered – and it is announced in good time.

beh12.q: You missed your exit on the motorway. What do you do?
a: Drive on to the next exit
Reverse on the hard shoulder
Turn round at a gap in the central reservation
beh12.why: On the motorway, turning round and reversing are forbidden – take the next exit.

beh13.q: You join the motorway from the slip road. Who goes first?
a: The traffic already on the motorway
You – the others must make room
Whoever is faster
beh13.why: Traffic on the motorway has the right of way. Match its speed on the acceleration lane and merge into a gap.

beh14.q: A child of 8 years, 1.30 m tall, rides in your car. What must it use?
a: A child seat that fits it
Only the normal seat belt
Nothing on the back seat
beh14.why: Children under 12 years and smaller than 150 cm ride in a child seat that suits their size and weight.

beh15.q: You drive into a roundabout with signs 215 and 205. When do you indicate?
a: Right, before you leave it
Left, as you enter
Not at all
beh15.why: Entering, you do not indicate. Before you leave, indicate right.

beh16.q: A bus at a stop has switched on its hazard lights. Children get off. How may you pass?
a: Only at walking pace
Only at a distance that puts nobody in danger
Normally, if the bus is on the other side of the road
beh16.why: Passing a bus that stands at its stop with hazard lights on: walking pace and room enough – that holds for the oncoming traffic as well.

pri01.q: A crossroads without signs or traffic lights. Who has priority?
a: Whoever comes from the right
Whoever arrived first
Whoever is on the wider road
pri01.why: Where nothing else is signed, right before left applies.

a: Give way to the traffic on the road you enter
Stop at the line in every case
You have priority at the next junction
pri02.why: Zeichen 205: give way – stop if needed, and let the traffic on the crossing road go first.

a: Stop completely at the stop line
Give way to the traffic on the crossing road
Slow down only if somebody comes
pri03.why: Zeichen 206: stop – always, even with nobody coming – and give way.

pri04.q: What does this sign tell you?
a: You have priority at the next junction only
You have priority until the sign that ends it
Others must stop
pri04.why: Zeichen 301 gives priority at the next crossing or junction – only there.

pri05.q: What does this sign tell you?
a: You are on a priority road
It lasts until it is ended or another rule is signed
Right before left applies
pri05.why: Zeichen 306: the priority road – it gives priority at every junction until it ends (Zeichen 307) or something else is signed.

pri06.q: Traffic lights show green, but a police officer stands in the junction and faces you with both arms out to the sides. What do you do?
a: Stop
Drive on: green comes first
Drive on, but slowly
pri06.why: The signs of the police come before traffic lights, signs and all other rules. Arms out, facing you: stop.

pri07.q: You want to turn left at a junction. A car comes towards you and goes straight on. Who goes first?
a: The oncoming car
You, if you were there first
You, if you have green
pri07.why: Turning left, let the oncoming traffic go first – also when you both have green.

pri08.q: You and an oncoming car both want to turn left at a crossroads. How do you turn?
a: In front of each other, without crossing behind
Behind each other, round the middle
One waits until the other has gone
pri08.why: Two left turners turn in front of each other unless the traffic or the markings say otherwise.

pri09.q: You drive out of a car park onto the road. Who goes first?
a: All the traffic on the road – also cyclists and people on foot
Whoever comes from the right
You, if you indicate
pri09.why: Coming from a property, a car park or over a lowered kerb you must put nobody in danger – you give way to everybody.

pri10.q: You want to turn off a road with tram tracks. A tram comes from behind and goes straight on in your direction. Who goes first?
a: The tram
You, because you are ahead
pri10.why: When you turn, trams going your way go first, also when they come from behind. Wait beside the tracks, not on them.

pri11.q: You come to a roundabout with these signs: the blue roundabout sign and give-way. Who goes first?
a: The traffic already in the roundabout
Whoever comes from the right
pri11.why: With Zeichen 215 and 205 the traffic in the roundabout has the right of way.

pri12.q: Your light is red. Beside it there is a green arrow pointing right. What may you do?
a: Turn right after stopping, if nobody is hindered or put in danger
Turn right without stopping
Drive straight on
pri12.why: The green arrow sign allows turning right on red – after stopping, and only without hindering or endangering anybody.

pri13.q: Your priority road bends to the left at the junction and you follow it. What is right?
a: Indicate left
You keep priority
You must give way to the road going straight on
pri13.why: Whoever follows a priority road that bends indicates; you keep the right of way.

a: Give way to oncoming traffic at the narrow stretch
You have priority over oncoming traffic
pri14.why: Zeichen 208: the oncoming traffic goes first through the narrow place – wait if it comes.

a: No more than 50 km/h
At least 50 km/h
50 km/h recommended
sig01.why: Zeichen 274: the highest speed allowed. It holds until it is lifted.

a: Cyclists and riders of mopeds
Cars
Motorcycles without a sidecar
sig02.why: Zeichen 276 forbids overtaking motor vehicles with more than one track – single-track vehicles may be overtaken.

a: Any stopping on the carriageway
Only parking
sig03.why: Zeichen 283: no stopping at all – not even to let somebody out.

sig04.q: What may you do under this sign?
a: Stop for up to three minutes
Let people in or out and load or unload, also longer
Park for up to an hour
sig04.why: Zeichen 286: stopping is allowed up to three minutes – longer only to let people in or out or to load and unload.

a: No entry for vehicles
One-way street
sig05.why: Zeichen 267: you may not drive in here.

a: Walking pace
Children may play everywhere on the road
Parking only in the marked places
sig06.why: In a traffic-calmed area (Zeichen 325.1) you drive at walking pace; people on foot may use the whole road, and parking is allowed only where marked.

sig07.q: This sign stands at the entrance of a residential area. What usually applies at its junctions?
a: Right before left
Priority for the road you are on
sig07.why: In a 30 km/h zone the junctions are usually without signs: right before left.

sig08.q: What does this sign warn of?
a: A level crossing
A tram stop
sig08.why: Zeichen 151 warns of a level crossing ahead.

sig09.q: What does this sign warn of?
a: Children – a school or a playground nearby
A zebra crossing
sig09.why: Zeichen 136: children. Slow down and be ready to brake.

a: People on foot
Adult cyclists
Cars
sig10.why: Zeichen 239: a footway – other traffic only where an added panel allows it (children on bicycles are an exception of their own).

sig11.q: What does this sign mean for cyclists?
a: They must use this cycle track
They may choose the road instead
sig11.why: Zeichen 237 marks a cycle track that cyclists must use.

sig12.q: How far before and after this sign may you not park?
a: 5 m
sig12.why: At a stop with Zeichen 224, parking is not allowed up to 15 m before and after the sign.

sig13.q: Which vehicles may use the road behind this sign?
a: Only motor vehicles built to go faster than 60 km/h
All motor vehicles
Bicycles too
sig13.why: Zeichen 330.1 begins the motorway: only for motor vehicles that can go faster than 60 km/h.

a: All speed limits and overtaking bans signed along the road
Only the motorway
sig14.why: Zeichen 282 ends all speed limits and overtaking bans that were signed for the stretch.

sig15.q: What does this added panel say?
a: The sign above it holds only when the road is wet
Danger of skidding always

sig16.q: Who may drive into a road with Zeichen 250 and this panel?
a: Those who live there or have business there
Everybody
Only cyclists
sig16.why: Anlieger frei: those who live or have something to do along the road – visiting, delivering – may drive in.

sig17.q: What does this sign tell you?
a: A dead end – the road does not go through
A car park

spd01.q: What is the highest speed for a car in town, without signs?
a: 50 km/h
30 km/h
60 km/h
spd01.why: In built-up areas 50 km/h applies to all vehicles unless a sign says otherwise.

spd02.q: What is the highest speed for a car outside town, without signs, not on the motorway?
a: 100 km/h
80 km/h
120 km/h
spd02.why: Outside built-up areas cars may drive 100 km/h – 80 km/h with a trailer.

spd03.q: Which speed is recommended on the motorway?
a: 130 km/h
120 km/h
There is none
spd03.why: On motorways without a limit 130 km/h is the recommended speed; drive faster and you may share the blame for an accident.

spd04.q: A car with a trailer, outside town on a country road. How fast may it go at most?
a: 80 km/h
100 km/h
60 km/h
spd04.why: Cars with a trailer may drive at most 80 km/h outside built-up areas, also on the motorway (100 km/h with the Tempo-100 approval).

spd05.q: With snow chains on, how fast may you drive at most? (km/h)
spd05.why: With snow chains on, 50 km/h is the most – also where more is allowed.

spd06.q: Rule of thumb: how long is the reaction distance at 50 km/h? (m)

spd07.q: Rule of thumb: how long is the normal braking distance at 50 km/h? (m)

spd08.q: Rule of thumb: how long is the stopping distance at 100 km/h, reacting and braking normally? (m)
spd08.why: Reaction 100 ÷ 10 × 3 = 30 m plus braking (100 ÷ 10)² = 100 m: 130 m.

spd09.q: You double your speed. What happens to the braking distance?
a: It becomes about four times as long
It doubles
It stays the same
spd09.why: The braking distance grows with the square of the speed: twice as fast, four times as far.

spd10.q: Outside town at 80 km/h, how much distance do you keep to the car ahead at least, by the rule of thumb? (m)
spd10.why: Half the speedometer in metres: 40 m at 80 km/h – about two seconds.

spd11.q: How fast may you drive at most when fog leaves you less than 50 m to see? (km/h)
spd11.why: Less than 50 m to see: no faster than 50 km/h – slower if need be.

spd12.q: When must you drive slower than the signs allow?
a: When the road is icy or wet
When you cannot see far
Never: the sign says the speed
spd12.why: The speed must suit the road, the traffic, the view and the weather. You must be able to stop within the distance you can see.

spd13.q: May you drive slowly without a reason and hold up the traffic behind you?
a: No
Yes, slow is always safe
spd13.why: Without a good reason, motor vehicles may not drive so slowly that they hinder the flow of traffic.

spd14.q: How do you approach a zebra crossing where somebody wants to cross?
a: Slowly, ready to stop
Let the person cross
Sound the horn and drive on
spd14.why: At a zebra crossing those who clearly want to cross must be let across: approach at moderate speed and stop if needed.

ovt01.q: On which side do you overtake as a rule?
a: On the left
On the right
Whichever is free
When the traffic situation is unclear
When you are going faster than the vehicle ahead
When an oncoming vehicle could be put in danger
ovt02.why: Overtaking is forbidden when the situation is unclear and when the oncoming traffic could be hindered or endangered.

ovt03.q: Overtaking a cyclist in town, how much room to the side must you leave at least? (m)
ovt03.why: At least 1.5 m in town – at least 2 m outside town.

ovt04.q: Overtaking a cyclist outside town, how much room to the side must you leave at least? (m)
ovt04.why: At least 2 m outside town – at least 1.5 m in town.

ovt05.q: Somebody overtakes you. What must you not do?
a: Speed up
Keep right
ovt05.why: Whoever is overtaken must not speed up.

ovt06.q: When may you overtake on the right?
a: When the car ahead has indicated left and moved to the middle to turn
In town on a road with several marked lanes your way
On a country road when the car ahead is too slow
ovt06.why: Overtaking on the right is allowed past somebody who has indicated and positioned to turn left, and in town where there are several marked lanes your way (cars and other vehicles up to 3.5 t).

ovt07.q: Before a level crossing (from Zeichen 151/156) – may you overtake motor vehicles?
a: No
Yes, if the barriers are open
ovt07.why: From the warning signs up to and over the level crossing, motor vehicles must not be overtaken.

ovt08.q: What do you do when pulling out to overtake and when coming back?
a: Indicate as you pull out and as you pull back in
Look in the mirrors and over your shoulder
Pull in again directly in front of the overtaken car
ovt08.why: Announce both moves with the indicator; pull back in only when the overtaken car cannot be hindered.

ovt09.q: A tram runs on rails in the middle of the road; your street is not a one-way street. On which side do you overtake it?
a: On the right
On the left
ovt09.why: Rail vehicles are overtaken on the right – on the left only in one-way streets or where there is no room on the right.

ovt10.q: May you overtake at a zebra crossing?
a: No
Yes, if nobody is on it
ovt10.why: At zebra crossings, overtaking is forbidden.

a: When you leave the car
When you stand longer than three minutes
When you switch off the engine
prk01.why: Whoever leaves the vehicle or stands longer than three minutes parks.

prk02.q: How far from the meeting point of the kerbs of a junction must you stay with a parked car? (m)
prk02.why: No parking within 5 m of junctions and crossroads – 8 m before it where a cycle track runs on the right.

a: On a zebra crossing and up to 5 m before it
At a narrow or unclear place
At the right-hand kerb of a straight, clear road without signs
prk03.why: No stopping at narrow and unclear places, in sharp bends, on level crossings, on zebra crossings and up to 5 m before them, among others.

prk04.q: On which side of a two-way road do you park?
a: On the right
On either side
prk04.why: Stop and park on the right; on the left only in one-way streets or where tram tracks lie on the right.

prk05.q: May you park in front of a driveway to a property?
a: No
Yes, for up to an hour
prk05.why: Parking in front of driveways is not allowed – on narrow roads also opposite them.

prk06.q: Where is stopping not allowed because of traffic lights or signs?
a: Up to 10 m before traffic lights if you would hide them
Up to 10 m before a stop or give-way sign if you would hide it
prk06.why: Up to 10 m before traffic lights and the signs 201, 205 and 206 you may not stop where you would hide them.

prk07.q: You arrive at 10:10 where a parking disc is needed. Which time do you set?
prk07.why: Set the disc to the next half hour after you arrive.

prk08.q: You leave your parked car. What must you do?
a: Secure it so that it cannot roll away
Make it hard to steal: windows shut, key with you
Leave the hazard lights on
prk08.why: Whoever leaves a vehicle secures it against rolling away and against misuse.

prk09.q: May you park on the pavement?
a: Only where a sign or the markings allow it
Always, half on it
prk09.why: Parking on the pavement is allowed only where it is signed or marked (for example Zeichen 315).

a: Parking
Stopping only
prk10.why: Zeichen 314: a car park or parking place; added panels may limit it.

lgt01.q: In a tunnel during the day – which lights?
a: Dipped headlights
No lights, it is lit
Full beam
lgt01.why: In a tunnel you drive with dipped headlights, however bright it is inside.

lgt02.q: When may you switch on the rear fog light?
a: Only when fog leaves you less than 50 m to see
Whenever it rains
At night on country roads
lgt02.why: The rear fog light only when you see less than 50 m because of fog – otherwise it dazzles those behind you.

lgt03.q: Somebody comes towards you at night while your full beam is on. What do you do?
a: Dip your lights in good time
Flash them twice
lgt03.why: Dip your lights in good time for oncoming traffic and when following closely.

lgt04.q: It rains so hard that you see badly – it is daytime. Which lights?
a: Dipped headlights
Only daytime running lights
lgt04.why: When fog, snow or rain impair the view, you need dipped headlights by day too.

lgt05.q: When do you switch on the hazard lights?
a: When you are broken down or towed
When you come to the end of a jam on a motorway
When you park for a moment in the second row
lgt05.why: Hazard lights: broken down, towed, approaching the end of a jam, and buses at their stops when the authority wants it.

lgt06.q: May you drive with parking lights only?
a: No
Yes, in a lit town
lgt06.why: Driving with parking lights only is not allowed.

lgt07.q: Outside town you want to say you are about to overtake. What may you use?
a: Short flashes of the headlights
The horn
The hazard lights
lgt07.why: Outside built-up areas overtaking may be announced with short flashes or the horn.

lgt08.q: You park at night on a country road outside town. What is needed?
a: The parking light or the lights of the vehicle to show where it stands
Nothing
lgt08.why: Vehicles standing at night must be lit where the road is not lit enough – outside town always.

lgt09.q: Do daytime running lights replace dipped headlights in the dark?
a: No
Yes
lgt09.why: In the dark, at dusk and in tunnels you need the dipped headlights – daytime running lights light up only the front.

lgt10.q: When may you use front fog lights?
a: When fog, snow or rain impair the view
Always at night
lgt10.why: Fog lights only when fog, snow or rain make it hard to see.

alc01.q: Which blood alcohol may a driver in the probation period have?
a: Up to 0.3 ‰
Up to 0.5 ‰
alc01.why: During the probation period and below 21 years: no alcohol at all when driving.

alc02.q: From which blood alcohol is driving an offence for everybody, even without signs of being unfit? (‰)
alc02.why: From 0.5 ‰ (or 0.25 mg/l in the breath) it is an administrative offence.

alc03.q: You have 0.4 ‰ and drive unsteadily. What can follow?
a: A criminal charge for drunk driving
Nothing, you are below 0.5 ‰
alc03.why: From 0.3 ‰ together with signs of being unfit to drive it is a criminal offence.

alc04.q: How can you lower your blood alcohol faster?
a: Not at all – only time helps
Strong coffee
Fresh air and a shower
alc04.why: The body breaks alcohol down at about 0.1 ‰ an hour; nothing speeds it up.

alc05.q: You take a medicine with a warning about driving. What do you do?
a: Read the leaflet and ask the doctor whether you may drive
Drive anyway, medicines are allowed
alc05.why: Medicines can make you unfit to drive; whoever drives unfit commits an offence.

alc06.q: You feel tired on a long drive. What is right?
a: Take a break and rest
Open the window and drive on
Drive faster to be home sooner
alc06.why: Whoever is unfit – tired too – may not drive. Take breaks in good time, about every two hours.

alc07.q: Which limit for THC (cannabis) in the blood serum applies to drivers? (ng/ml)
alc07.why: From 3.5 ng/ml THC in the blood serum driving is an offence; mixing cannabis with alcohol is forbidden altogether, and novices may not drive with any.

alc08.q: How long is the probation period of a new licence?
a: 2 years
1 year
5 years
alc08.why: Two years. After one serious or two less serious violations a seminar for novice drivers is ordered – and the probation period grows by two years, to four.

alc09.q: From how many points in the register in Flensburg is the licence taken away? (points)
alc09.why: With 8 points the licence is withdrawn.

alc10.q: Which effects does alcohol have even in small amounts?
a: You react later
You see less to the sides
You take more risks
alc10.why: Even small amounts slow reactions, narrow the field of view and make you bolder.

env01.q: May you let the engine run while you stand and wait?
a: No
Yes, to warm it up
env01.why: Unnecessary noise and exhaust are forbidden – also warming the engine up standing still.

a: Change up early
Drive with foresight and roll
Drive in low gears at high revs
env02.why: Low revs and smooth driving with foresight save fuel.

a: Tyre pressure too low
An empty roof box left on
Driving at an even speed
env03.why: Soft tyres and drag from things on the roof cost fuel.

env04.q: Is driving up and down the same street for no reason allowed in town?
a: No
Yes
env04.why: Driving needlessly back and forth in towns is forbidden when it disturbs others.

env05.q: The engine is cold. What do you do?
a: Drive off at once, gently
Let it idle for a few minutes first
env05.why: Drive off gently straight away: the engine warms up fastest that way – idling only makes exhaust.

env06.q: What do you need to drive into an environmental zone?
a: The right sticker on the windscreen
Nothing
env06.why: In an environmental zone (Zeichen 270.1) only vehicles with the sticker named on the sign may drive.

env07.q: Where do you leave old engine oil?
a: At a collection point or where new oil is sold
In the drain
env07.why: Old oil is hazardous waste: shops that sell oil take it back.

env08.q: How does speed affect fuel use?
a: Fuel use rises sharply at high speed
It makes no difference
env08.why: Air drag grows with the square of the speed – driving fast costs much more fuel.

env09.q: What helps the environment on a short trip in town?
a: Walking, cycling or the bus
Driving short distances only with a cold engine
env09.why: Short trips with a cold engine cause the most exhaust per kilometre.

env10.q: You wait at a level crossing with the barriers down for a long time. What do you do?
a: Switch the engine off
Keep it running
env10.why: Where you wait for longer, switch the engine off – needless exhaust is forbidden.

tec01.q: What is the least tread depth of car tyres allowed by law? (mm)
tec01.why: At least 1.6 mm – much more is safer on wet roads and in winter.

tec02.q: When do you need winter tyres?
a: When there is black ice, snow, slush or frost on the road
From October to Easter, whatever the weather
tec02.why: In wintry conditions only tyres with the alpine symbol are allowed.

tec03.q: What does ABS do in an emergency stop?
a: You can still steer while braking hard
The braking distance is always shorter
tec03.why: ABS keeps the wheels from locking, so the car can still be steered – it does not always shorten the distance.

tec04.q: Which things must be in every car?
a: A warning triangle
A first-aid kit
A high-visibility vest
tec04.why: Triangle, first-aid kit and a high-visibility vest belong in every car.

tec05.q: The red oil-pressure warning light comes on while you drive. What do you do?
a: Stop as soon as it is safe and switch off the engine
Drive on to the next garage
tec05.why: Without oil pressure the engine is damaged within moments.

tec06.q: When do you check the tyre pressure?
a: With the tyres cold
After a long drive at high speed
tec06.why: Check cold tyres; raise the pressure for a heavy load as the manual says.

tec07.q: How often does a private car go to the main inspection (HU)?
a: Every 2 years, the first time after 3 years
Every year
tec07.why: A new car first after three years, then every two years.

tec08.q: You drive down a long, steep hill. How do you keep your speed down?
a: Use a lower gear and the engine's braking
Brake all the time
tec08.why: Braking all the way down overheats the brakes – they fade.

tec09.q: Why must brake fluid be changed from time to time?
a: It takes up water and boils sooner
It gets thicker
tec09.why: Brake fluid draws in water over time – vapour bubbles can make the pedal go soft.

tec10.q: Which tasks do the seat belt and the headrest have?
a: The belt holds you in the seat in a crash
The headrest protects the neck – its top at about the height of your head's top
tec10.why: Adjust the headrest high enough; buckle up on every trip.

tec11.q: The coolant temperature warning comes on. What do you do?
a: Stop, let the engine cool down, check the coolant
Open the radiator cap at once
tec11.why: Hot coolant is under pressure – open the cap only when the engine has cooled.

a: It brakes single wheels to keep the car from skidding
It lets you drive faster round bends than physics allows
tec12.why: ESP helps within the limits of the tyres' grip – it cannot move those limits.

clb01.q: Up to which permissible total mass may you drive a vehicle with class B? (kg)
clb01.why: Class B: motor vehicles up to 3,500 kg permissible total mass, with no more than eight seats besides the driver's.

clb02.q: With class B, which trailer may you tow?
a: A trailer of up to 750 kg permissible total mass
A heavier one if the combination stays within 3,500 kg
Any trailer
clb02.why: Class B covers trailers up to 750 kg, or heavier ones when the whole combination stays within 3,500 kg.

clb03.q: How many seats may a class B vehicle have besides the driver's at most?
clb03.why: No more than eight seats besides the driver's.

clb04.q: Your load sticks out more than 1 m at the back. What is needed?
a: A light-red flag or plate at its end
At dusk and night a red light there as well
Nothing
clb04.why: Load sticking out more than 1 m beyond the rear reflectors is marked at its end – a light-red flag or plate (or cylinder), and when lights are needed a red light and a red reflector.

clb05.q: How must the load be stowed?
a: So that it cannot slip, fall over or fall off even when braking hard or swerving
Only so that it does not fall off at normal speeds
clb05.why: Load is secured against slipping, toppling, rolling and falling – also in an emergency stop or a sudden swerve.

clb06.q: You tow a broken-down car with a rope. What is right?
a: A rope at most 5 m long, made clearly visible
Hazard lights on both cars
On the motorway: leave it at the next exit
clb06.why: Towing: a clearly visible rope up to 5 m, hazard lights on, and off the motorway at the next exit.

clb07.q: Your trailer starts to sway on the motorway. What do you do?
a: Take your foot off the accelerator, hold the wheel steady
Brake firmly once the combination runs straight
Accelerate to pull it straight
clb07.why: Speeding up makes it worse. Slow down, hold steady, brake when straight.

clb08.q: At which age may you drive a car accompanied (BF17)? (years)
clb08.why: From 17, with an approved companion named in the certificate.

clb09.q: Which classes does a class B licence include?
a: AM
L
A1
clb09.why: Class B includes classes AM and L.

clb10.q: You load heavy things into the boot and onto the roof. What changes?
a: The braking distance grows
The car leans more in bends and is blown about more
Nothing
clb10.why: Load changes braking, steering and the wind's effect. Put heavy things low and forward; mind the roof load the manual allows.

clb11.q: Who is responsible for the safe state of the car and its load while you drive?
a: You, the driver
Only the owner
The garage
clb11.why: The driver answers for a roadworthy vehicle, a secure load and a clear view.

clb12.q: How high may a car with its load be at most? (m)
clb12.why: Vehicle and load together may be no higher than 4 m.

rbl.q: A crossroads without signs. Two other cars come towards it from the sides.
a: The car from the right has priority and may drive into the crossroads
The car from the left may not have seen you
Your lane is a priority road
rbl.why: Without signs right before left applies – and you cannot be sure the others know it.

bend.q: You follow the priority road round to the left. A car waits at the side road.
a: The waiting car may pull out because it thinks you go straight on
Your indicator may be overlooked
Nobody may cross your way
bend.why: Whoever waits must give way – but people misjudge where a car on a bending priority road is going.

leftTurn.q: You wait in the junction to turn left. A car comes towards you.
a: The oncoming car goes first
A cyclist may come behind the oncoming car
You may turn now: you have green
leftTurn.why: Turning left you let all oncoming traffic go first – also what is hidden behind it.

zebra.q: A person walks towards the zebra crossing ahead.
a: She clearly wants to cross and has priority
She may step onto the crossing at any moment
She must wait until you have passed
zebra.why: Anyone who clearly wants to use a zebra crossing must be let across.

tram.q: You wait to turn left beside the tram tracks. A tram comes from behind.
a: The tram goes straight on and has priority
Your car must not stand on the tracks
The tram will stop for you
tram.why: When you turn, trams going your way go first, also from behind.

corridor.q: Two lanes, the traffic slows down to walking pace.
a: The cars ahead may stop suddenly
An emergency vehicle may need a corridor
It is a good moment to change lanes
corridor.why: In a slowing queue, brake in good time and keep space for the emergency corridor.

schoolBus.q: A school bus stands at its stop with hazard lights on.
a: Children may run across the road
Children may step out from in front of the bus
Children always wait until the bus has gone
schoolBus.why: At a bus with hazard lights: walking pace, ready to stop – children often cross behind or in front of it.

overtake.q: A cyclist rides ahead of you, a car comes towards you.
a: There is not enough room to overtake the cyclist now
The cyclist may swerve round a drain or a pothole
You must overtake before the car comes
overtake.why: Overtake only with room to the side and without danger to oncoming traffic – here stay behind.

blindSpot.q: You want to turn right. A cyclist rides up on the cycle lane beside you.
a: The cyclist may be in your blind spot
The cyclist goes straight on and has priority
Your mirror shows everything
blindSpot.why: Before turning right, look over your shoulder: cyclists going straight on go first.

zip.q: Your lane ends ahead, the left lane is full.
a: Cars may push into your lane unexpectedly
Cars ahead of you may stop to merge
Nobody will change lanes before the end
zip.why: Where lanes merge, others misjudge the zip – be ready for sudden braking and cutting in.

motorway.q: You are on the acceleration lane, a lorry beside you.
a: The lorry has priority and will not move over
The acceleration lane ends
The lorry must let you in
motorway.why: The motorway traffic goes first: match your speed and slot in behind the lorry if need be.

roundabout.q: A red car comes round the roundabout.
a: Traffic in the roundabout has priority
The red car may not leave at the exit you think
You may drive in: you come from the right
roundabout.why: Traffic in the roundabout goes first – and you cannot be sure where it leaves until it does.

greenArrow.q: Red light with the green arrow. Somebody crosses on their green.
a: People crossing on green go first
You must stop first in any case
The arrow gives you priority
greenArrow.why: The green arrow only allows turning after stopping, without hindering anybody.

parkingSigns.q: You drive along a street with no-stopping signs; your passenger wants to get out.
a: You may not stop here, not even briefly
Cars behind you do not expect you to stop
A short stop is always allowed
parkingSigns.why: Under Zeichen 283 no stopping at all – the traffic behind you counts on it.

followingDistance.q: You follow a red car on a country road at 60 km/h.
a: It may brake hard at any moment
You need the distance to react and to brake
Two car lengths are enough at this speed
followingDistance.why: Keep enough distance to stop even when the car ahead brakes suddenly: at 60 km/h at least 30 m.

narrowPass.q: A lorry has broken down in your lane, a car comes towards you.
a: The obstacle is on your side: you wait
Somebody may walk round the lorry
The oncoming car must wait for you
narrowPass.why: Whoever has the obstacle on their side lets the oncoming traffic through first.

busStopPullOut.q: A bus stands at its stop, people get off.
a: People may cross in front of the bus
The bus may pull out
The bus never moves while you pass
busStopPullOut.why: Pass a bus at its stop slowly and let it leave the stop if it wants to.

nightDrive.q: Night on a country road. With dipped headlights you see only some 50 m.
a: People in dark clothes are seen very late
You must stop within the reach of your lights
The road ahead is surely empty
nightDrive.why: At night drive no faster than lets you stop within the distance you can see.

a: Slow cars ahead may appear suddenly
You see less than 50 m
Full beam will help you see
fogWall.why: With less than 50 m to see: at most 50 km/h, dipped lights, the rear fog light allowed.

accidentScene.q: Two crashed cars stand on the country road ahead.
a: People may be on the road
Traffic behind you may not see the accident yet
The accident is over: nothing more can happen
accidentScene.why: Warn the traffic behind with your hazard lights, stop well back and make the place safe.

truckBlindSpot.q: A lorry waits to turn right, a cyclist rolls up beside it.
a: The lorry driver may not see the cyclist
The lorry may start turning
Lorries have mirrors that show everything
truckBlindSpot.why: From the high cab the cyclist is hard to see – keep back and let the turn play out.

multiLane.q: The blue car beside you indicates left – into your lane, though there is no room.
a: It may change lanes anyway
Braking hard could get you hit from behind
It has priority because it indicated
multiLane.why: Whoever changes lanes must make sure nobody is endangered – but expect others to make mistakes.

tunnel.q: A country road leads into a tunnel; it is daytime.
a: Your eyes need time to adapt to the dark
A broken-down car may stand in the tunnel
Nothing changes in the tunnel
tunnel.why: In a tunnel drive with dipped headlights and keep your distance.

seniorCrossing.q: An old lady with a rollator steps off the kerb.
a: She is slow and may stop on the road
She may not have seen you
She will hurry once she sees you
seniorCrossing.why: With old people, slow down and be ready to brake – so that no danger can arise for them.

wildlife.q: Dusk in a forest. A deer stands at the edge of the road.
a: It may jump onto the road
More animals may follow it
Deer always run away from cars
wildlife.why: Wild animals react unpredictably; where one is, others follow.

policeSignals.q: A police officer stands in the crossroads, the lights work.
a: His signs come before the lights
He may stop you although your light is green
The lights come first
policeSignals.why: The signs of the police come before traffic lights and all other rules.

flagman.q: Roadworks close your lane; a man with a stop/go sign regulates the traffic.
a: Workers may step into your way
Oncoming cars use the one open lane
You may pass as long as nobody comes
flagman.why: Wait at his red side – the one open lane belongs to the oncoming traffic now; then drive slowly past the workers.

levelCrossing.q: A level crossing ahead; a train is coming.
a: The lights may turn yellow and red
A train cannot stop or swerve
You may still cross while the light is yellow
levelCrossing.why: Yellow or red at a level crossing: wait before the St Andrew's cross.

levelCrossingQueue.q: Behind the level crossing the traffic stands still.
a: You might have to stop on the tracks
The barriers may close
A queue always moves on in time
levelCrossingQueue.why: Cross only when you can get all the way over without stopping.
